9.5a — Datasets: Insights from Playtest Data

All semester you have written playtest numbers in tables (6.5a, 7.7a). Today those habits become DATA SCIENCE: one shared dataset of 32 playtest runs, real questions, and the move from "I feel like the spike room is hard" to "the spike room is where 62% of deaths happen."

Concept Lab ~15 min

Download the dataset. Grab playtests.csv — 32 runs, 6 sections, one row per playtester per run. Each column is a variable; each row is one record. The columns:

ColumnMeaning
sectionWhich part of the cave (1=entrance … 6=boss door)
run_id, player_idWhich run, which tester
deaths, deaths_by_spikes, deaths_by_enemy, deaths_by_fallDeath counts BY CAUSE
time_secondsTime in that section
coins_missedCoins the tester saw but did not get
jumpsJump inputs pressed (activity!)
distance_to_boss_startHow far into section 6 they died/gave up
completed_boss1 = won the fight, 0 = did not
rating (1–5), commentFelt experience, in their words

Socratic

The exam's dataset questions hinge on knowing WHICH column answers WHICH question. "Which section is deadliest?" uses deaths; "which section FRUSTRATES?" needs time PLUS rating. Why can the deadliest section and the most-hated section be different — and what would a designer do differently about each?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — eyeball then compute. Open the CSV in any spreadsheet tool (Numbers, Google Sheets). Predict three things from eyeballing, THEN compute them: total deaths per section (sort/sum), average time per section, and the completion rate (completed_boss column: what fraction is 1?). A prediction next to a result is the whole scientific method in one spreadsheet.

Step 2 — cross-tab questions. The interesting questions join columns:

  1. Do high-jump sections have more fall deaths? (jumps vs. deaths_by_fall, per row)
  2. Do testers who miss more coins rate lower? (coins_missed vs. rating)
  3. Which section has the WORST time-per-death ratio (slow AND deadly = the frustration zone)?
  4. Of testers who died to the enemy, what fraction still beat the boss? (deaths_by_enemy > 0, then completed_boss)

Step 3 — aggregate like the exam. AP pseudocode loves AVERAGE and SUM over filtered lists. Do the section-2 average time BY HAND as a filtered list: keep rows where section == 2, average time_seconds. Write it in exam pseudocode next to your spreadsheet answer:

times ← [row.time_seconds FOR row IN runs IF row.section = 2]
AVERAGE(times)

Bug Hunt: Data traps

  1. One tester ran section 3 four times (four rows). Compare their 4 times: why is the FIRST run's time a different KIND of number than the fourth (learning effect — what does that mean for "average difficulty")?
  2. A row shows rating 5, deaths 7. What is that row telling you — and why does "hard but loved" exist (see 7.5a: hard-but-fair vs easy-but-random)?
  3. Sort by deaths descending. The top row: what should you READ before you act — deaths, time, OR the comment? Why is the comment the only column that explains the number?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: One insight, one change

  1. Write ONE insight as a full sentence with numbers: "Testers died 2× more in section ___ than any other, and their comments mention ___."
  2. Then ONE design change to YOUR cave that the insight implies — and nothing else. (The discipline of one-variable changes, now driven by data instead of vibes — this is the loop the whole year has been practicing.)
  3. Hard: which column is MISSING that would settle the biggest open question about your boss fight? (Propose it — a column is a design decision.)

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name variable vs record and read a CSV fluently
  • Answer cross-column questions with spreadsheet filters/aggregates
  • Express a filtered average in AP pseudocode
  • Turn one dataset insight into one design change
